strengths: Addresses an important deployment problem: estimating performance when production labels are unavailable or delayed. The method uses reference labels, production features, and stored model outputs without requiring queries to the monitored model.

Combining density-ratio weighting with score calibration is a simple, potentially useful refinement of CBPE. The change-of-measure motivation is sound under covariate shift and adequate support overlap.

The empirical study is substantial within census data: 603 model–dataset pairs, 34,953 production chunks, and three classifier families. Table 1 reports consistently better aggregate errors than IW and CBPE across accuracy, AUROC, and F1. Evaluation also covers alert detection and chunk-size sensitivity.

Public datasets, pseudocode, and a repository link support reproducibility. The discussion candidly identifies concept shift, support mismatch, and limited effective sample size as limitations. Funding is disclosed, and no material ethical concern is evident.
weaknesses: The central guarantee in Sections 2.2–2.3 is invalid as stated. Calibration of fc does not suffice for evaluating decisions based on the original f. For example, two equally likely inputs with scores 0.25/0.75 and labels 0/1 have true thresholded accuracy 1, yet the perfectly calibrated constant map fc=0.5 makes Equation (3) estimate 0.5. This contradicts the claimed calibration-error bound even without distribution shift. Additional conditions linking calibration to the original scores or decisions are required; the weighted-regression specification does not establish them.

Appendix A interchanges true negatives and false negatives: TN should use (1-c(f))(1-rho(f)), while FN should use c(f)(1-rho(f)). These quantities affect F1 and ROC calculations. The paper must establish whether this is only a presentation error or also affects the experiments. Furthermore, nonlinear metrics such as F1 and AUROC do not automatically inherit the stated bound for observation-level metrics.

The alert evaluation contains a material inconsistency. Section 4.2 describes a prediction threshold of 3 SE, but Table 3 reports accuracy-alert F1=0.65 for M-CBPE, whereas Figure 3A shows roughly 0.58 at 3 SE and reaches 0.65 near 2 SE. Threshold selection, including any use of production labels, needs clarification. The definition of a positive prediction also improperly refers to both true and estimated changes if read literally.

Essential implementation details are absent from the manuscript, including the DRE and calibrator model families, hyperparameters, and treatment of extreme weights. Algorithm 1 fits DRE and evaluates it on the same reference inputs, making overfitting control particularly relevant. The repository link is helpful, but the central choices underlying the reported results and their sensitivity need documentation.

The experiments do not adequately establish the robustness or breadth of the superiority claims. All cases come from five related binary Folktables tasks, with shared observations across classifier families. There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated-run results, or task/model breakdowns for the improvements over IW; pooling chunks also gives larger datasets greater influence. Temporal census shifts are not established to preserve P(Y|X), and no controlled covariate-shift experiment isolates the claimed mechanism.

The methodological originality is primarily the composition of established density-ratio estimation and calibration techniques, with the theoretical foundations attributed to prior work. The paper needs a sharper explanation of its new insight and when the composition should improve on IW. Comparisons with accuracy-oriented ATC/DoC adaptations for F1 and AUROC also require stronger justification. The useful empirical contribution does not currently outweigh the theoretical and evaluation shortcomings.
